lawyer:
TH Khan with Md Ahasan, Advocates—For Petitioners.
Md Khurshedul Alam, Deputy Attorney General with Delowar Hossain Somadder, Assistant Attorney General and Manjur Kader, Assistant Attorney General—For the Opposite-Party No. 1. Md lqbal Kabir, Advocate—For the Opposite-Party No. 2.
parties:
Soumitra Sankar Das and another ----- Petitioner
Vs
State and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J : On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 filed by the petitioners, a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the proceedings of the Sessions Case No. 342 of 2010 arising out of Sadar CR Case No. 1100 of 2009 dated 6-12-2009 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, now pending before the Joint Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet should not be quashed and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 The accused-petitioners are the directors of the Kaltimex Energy Bangladesh (Pvt) Limited. This Company is engaged in establishing electrical power plants, power stations and deals in electrical instruments, gas generators etc. The Company is a local agent of MWM Asia Pacific (Pvt) Limited, 11, Teck Road, Singapore, which is affiliated to the world famous MWM, Gmbh, Carl Benz Str. 1, Mannheim, Germany, having unique reputation in business relating to electrical goods and in establishing power plants. Anyway, at one stage, the Shahjahan Ullah Power Generation Company Limited wanted to establish a 20MW gas-based power plant and in this regard, they through their chairman Mr Md Ata Ullah made a proposal to the Kaltimex Energy Bangladesh (Pvt) Limited. Accordingly, an indent was given with a view to establishing the power plant. On 5-1-2009 the Chief Executive of the Kaltimex informed the Shahjahan Ullah Power Generation Company Limited of the price of the establishment of the proposed power plant and a tripartite agreement was signed on 2-2-2009. As per terms of the agreement dated 2-2-2009, an amount equivalent to 1,00,000 (one lakh) euro was paid to the Kaltimex for onward transmission to the principal supplier, namely, MWM, Gmbh of Germany and that was in due course. However, on the request of Mr Md Ata Ullah, chairman of the Shahjahan Ullah Power Generation Company Limited, the Kaltimex gave a post-dated cheque to him for a sum of Taka 1,40,00,000 (one crore and forty lakh) only as security for performing the remaining work of the establishment of the power plant. But the Shahjahan Ullah Power Generation Company Limited authority failed to perform their part of the contractual obligations and no irrevocable letter of credit was opened within the given time-frame as agreed upon and that being so, the advance payment was fortified in accordance with the terms of the agreement. For and on behalf of the Kaltimex, the accused-petitioners jointly issued the cheque bearing No. 1495438 dated 15-4-2009 to be drawn upon the Company's Account No. 205-100-4086 of Dhaka Bank Limited. The cheque was presented to the bank for encashment on 23-9-2009 and 24-9-2009 and on both the dates, the cheque was dishonoured on the ground of insufficiency of funds. Lastly, on 27-9-2009 the cheque was again presented to the bank for encashment and on that date, the cheque was dishonoured on the score that the operation of the account had been stopped by the drawer. Subsequently, the opposite-party No.2 (Mr Md Ata Ullah) issued a legal notice on 11-10-2009 and that was served on the petitioners through its publication in 'The Daily Prothom Alo' on the self-same date demanding payment of the amount from them. But he failed to make the payment as demanded in the legal notice within the statutory period of 30 (thirty) days. Thereafter on expiration of 30 (thirty) days from the date of receipt of the notice, the opposite-party No. 2 on his own behalf and on behalf of Zahir Bakth instituted CR Case No. 1109 in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Sylhet under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as the Act of 1881) and the Court below took cognizance of the offence against the petitioners there under. Being aggrieved at and dissatisfied with the Order of taking cognizance against the petitioners, they approached the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained the instant Rule. 

 3. At the outset, Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioners, submits that admittedly the Company is a juristic person; but curiously enough, the Company has not been made an accused in this case as required under section 140(1) of the Act of 1881, though the petitioners issued the cheque for and on behalf of the 'Company and the non-impleading of the Company, that is to say, Kaltimex as an accused in the case has rendered the proceedings thereof incompetent in the Court below and this being the position, the proceedings are an abuse of the process of the Court and, as such, those are liable to be quashed. 

 4. Mr TH Khan next submits that sub-section (3) of section 138 of the Act of 1881 contemplates that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-sections (1) and (2), the holder of the cheque shall retain his right to establish his claim through the civil Court if whole or any part of the value of the cheque remains unrealized and in this view of the matter, it cannot be said that the opposite-party No. 2 will be left without remedy if the proceedings of the case are quashed to secure the ends of justice. 

 6. Mr TH Khan further submits that section 138 of the Act of 1881 provides that where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of the Act of 1881, be punished with the imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to thrice the amount of the cheque, or with both; and in the present case, admittedly the drawer of the cheque is a Company (Kaltimex) and the account is that of the Kaltimex and it does not belong to the petitioners in their personal capacity and in that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the legal notice was served upon the Company and such being the state of affairs, it is prima facie that the legal notice was not served upon the drawer (Kaltimex) and by that reason, the proceedings of the case pending in the Court below are an abuse of the process of the Court and from this standpoint, the proceedings ought to be quashed. 

 7. Mr TH Khan also submits that according to section 140 of the Act of 1881, if the person committing an offence under section 138 is a Company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the Company for the conduct of the business of the Company, as well as the Company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly; but the petition of complaint as well as the sworn statement recorded under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are conspicuously silent as to how the accused-petitioners were responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company and in the absence of such averment therein, the proceedings of the case being an abuse of the process of the Court cannot be continued and the same are, therefore, liable to be quashed. 

 8. Mr TH Khan next submits that the expression 'as well as the Company' occurring in section 140 (1) of the Act of 1881 shall have to be construed and interpreted, regard being had to the scheme of the Act and in the facts and circumstances of the present case and it appears from the language employed in sub-section (1) of section 140 that the Company is the principal offender and in the absence of the Company, the other alleged offenders, if any, cannot be fastened with the criminal liability under section 138 of the Act of 1881 and against this backdrop, the proceedings of the case should be quashed. 

 11. In support of the above submissions, Mr TH Khan draws our attention to the decisions in the cases of Ferdous Khan @ Alamgir vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd, 63 DLR 540 and K Srikanth Singh vs North East Securities Ltd, 2007 (8) SCR 452. 

 12. Per contra, Mr Md Iqbal Kabir, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the complainant-opposite-party No. 2, submits that through inadvertence, the Company (Kaltimex) has not been made an accused in the case in accordance with section 140(1) of the Act of 1881; but even then, the proceedings not being an abuse of the process of the Court are maintainable. 

 13. Mr Md Iqbal Kabir further submits that for non-impleading of the Company as an accused in the case, its proceedings cannot be quashed and the liability of the petitioners as the directors of the Company (Kaltimex) under section 138 of the Act of 1881 cannot be eschewed in that they are the admitted signatories to the bounced cheque. 

 14. Mr Md Iqbal Kabir next submits that as the indisputable directors of the Kaltimex the petitioners issued the cheque and the same was dishonoured thrice and thereafter the opposite-party No. 2 complied with all the legal formalities as postulated by section 138 of the Act of 1881 and since the petitioners failed to make the payment within the statutory period of 30 (thirty) days, opposite-party No. 2 lodged the petition of complaint with the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate of Sylhet as per law and on this count, no exception can be taken to the proceedings of the case and, in such a situation, the proceedings of the case cannot be quashed. 

 17. Mr Md Iqbal Kabir further submits that in a case under section 138 of the Act of 1881, this Court will only see whether there was bouncing of the cheque due to insufficiency of funds in the account of the Company and whether the opposite-party No. 2 complied with all legal formalities prior to initiation of the case before the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate of Sylhet and the proceedings of the case pending before him cannot be quashed on the basis of the defence materials, that is to say, alleged failure of the opposite-party No. 2 to open the letter of credit pursuant to the tripartite agreement dated 2-2-2009. 

 18. Mr Md Iqbal Kabir also submits that the non-impleading of the Company (Kaltimex) is a mere technical flaw and on this score alone, the proceedings of the case pending in the lower Court cannot be quashed and the cause of substantial justice demands that the petitioners, face trial in the case under section 138 of the Act of 1881 for their criminal liability as the directors of the Company. 

 19. Mr Md Iqbal Kabir next submits that it is a bona fide mistake in the petition of complaint that there is a reference to the petitioners Account No. 250-4086 with Dhaka Bank Limited instead of the Kaltimex's account therewith and the petitioners cannot derive any benefit out of this bona fide mistake in this case. 

 20. In support of the above submissions, Mr Md Iqbal Kabir relies on the decisions in the cases of Bimal Kumar Nopani vs State of Uttar Pradesh, 2006 (2) DCR 691; Rajneesh Aggarwal vs Amit J Bhalla, 2001 SCC (Crl) 229; M Venkatesh-wara Rao vs Medarametla Venkateshwarlu, 1984-1997 DCR (1) 416; Anil Hada vs Indian Acrylic Ltd, (2000) 1 SCC 1, SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd vs Neeta Bhalla, (2005) 8 SCC 89; P Pollution Control Board vs Messrs Modi Distillery, 1987 SCC (CrI) 632; Faridul Alam vs State, 16 BLT (AD) 51 Rahela Khatun vs Abul Hassan, 48 DLR (AD) 213. 

 24. In order to dilate upon the scope of a proceeding under section 561A of the Code, the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 may be referred to. In that decision, the Appellate Division clearly spelt out the categories of cases where the High Court Division should interfere under section 561A of the Code. In that decision, the Appellate Division observed as follows : 

 (a) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts, no case can stand against the accused. Where institution or continuance of criminal proceedings against an accused person may amount to an abuse of the process of the Court or when the quashing of the impugned 

 (c) Where there is a legal bar against institution or continuance of a criminal case against an accused person; 

 (d) In a case where the allegations in the First Information Report or the Complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirely, do not constitute the offence alleged and in such cases, no question of weighing and appreciating evidence arises; and 

 (e) The allegations made against the accused person do constitute an offence alleged; but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 25. The above-mentioned categories of cases as spelt out by our Appellate Division in the aforesaid decision reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 was subsequently followed in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, reported in 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16. 

 26. In the case of Sher Ali vs State reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67, the Appellate Division has held that the inherent power may be invoked independent of powers conferred by any other provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and this power may be exercised to quash a proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial if the Court concerned had no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on 'no evidence' or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. 

 27. Reverting to the case in hand, there is no gainsaying the fact that the drawer is the Company (Kaltimex). Undeniably, the petitioners are the paid directors of the Company and signatories to the cheque. We are concerned with the criminal liability on account of the dishonour of the cheque. It primarily falls on the drawer Company and is extended to the officers of the Company. The normal rule in the cases involving criminal liability is against vicarious liability, that is, no one is to be held criminally liable for an act of another. This normal rule is, however, subject to exceptions on account of specific provisions being engrafted in the statutes extending liability to others. Section 140 of the Act of 1881 is an instance of specific provision which, in case an offence under section 138 is committed by a Company, extends criminal liability for dishonour of a cheque to the officers of the Company. Section 140 contains conditions which have to be satisfied before the liability can be extended to the officers of the Company. As the provision creates criminal liability, the conditions have to be strictly complied with. The conditions are intended to ensure that a person, who is sought to be made vicariously liable for an offence of which the principal accused is the Company, had a role to play in relation to the incriminating act and further that he should know what is attributed to him to make him liable. In other words, persons who had nothing to do with the matter need not be roped in. A Company being a juristic person, all its deeds and functions are the result of the acts of others. Therefore, the officers of the Company who are responsible for the acts done in the name of the Company are sought to be made personally liable for the acts which result in a criminal action being taken against the Company. It makes every person, who at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the Company for the conduct of its business, as well as the Company, liable for the offence. The proviso to section 140(1) contains an escape route for the persons who are able to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. 

 28. The position of a Managing Director or a Joint Managing Director or a Deputy Managing Director of a Company is different from that of a mere Director. The Managing Director or the Joint Managing Director or the Deputy Managing Director, as the designation of their office suggests, are in charge of the Company and are responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company. In order to ward off criminal liability, such persons may have to bring their case within the proviso to section 140(1) of the Act of 1881. 

 30. In the decision in the case of Ferdous Khan @ Alamgir vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd, reported in 63 DLR 540 relied upon by Mr TH Khan, it has been held that for not making any allegation in the complaint petition of committing any offence under section 138 by the drawer-Company, the provisions of section 140 of the Act of 1881 would not be applicable and there is no scope in law to initiate or continue the proceeding or to hold the accused guilty in the case. It seems that this decision is the trump card of Mr TH Khan. For all practical purposes, the 'ratio' enunciated therein is the epicenter of all his submissions. Besides, the sheet-anchor of Mr TH Khan is the decision of the Indian Supreme Court reported in 2007 (8) SCR 452 (supra) which was downloaded from the internet. In that decision, the Indian Supreme Court referred to the case of Sabitha Ramamurthy vs RSS Channabasavamdhya, (2006) 10 SCC 581 quoted paragraph 7 with approval: 

 "7. A bare perusal of the complaint petition demonstrates that the statutory requirements contained in section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act had not been complied with. It may be true that it is not necessary for the complainant to specifically reproduce the wordings of the section; but what is required is a clear statement of fact so as to enable the Court to arrive at a prima facie opinion that the accused are vicariously liable. Section 141 raises a legal fiction. By reason of the said provision, a person although is not personally liable for commission of such an offence would be vicariously liable there for. Such vicarious liability can be inferred so far as a Company registered or incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 is concerned only if the requisite statements, which are required to be averred in the complaint petition, are made so as to make the accused therein vicariously liable for the offence committed by the Company. Before a person can be made vicariously liable, strict compliance with the statutory requirements would be insisted. Not only the averments made in para 7 of the complaint petition do not meet the said statutory requirements, the sworn statement of the witness made by the son of the respondent herein, does not contain any statement that the appellants were in charge of the business of the Company. In a case where the Court is required to issue summons which would put the accused to some sort of harassment, the Court should insist on strict compliance with the statutory requirements. In terms of section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the complainant is bound to make statements on oath as to how the offence has been committed and how the accused persons are responsible there for. In the event, ultimately, the prosecution is found to be frivolous or otherwise mala fide, the Court may direct registration of a case against the complainant for mala fide prosecution of the accused. The accused would also be entitled to file a suit for damages. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure are required to be construed from the aforementioned point of view". 

 32. Let us address the decision in the case of SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd vs Neeta Bhalla, (2005) 8 SCC 89 adverted to by Mr Md Iqbal Kabir. It is a larger Bench decision of the Indian Supreme Court. In that decision of the larger Bench of the Indian Supreme Court, the following three questions were posed for answer on a reference made by a two-Judge Bench of the said Court: 

 "10 While analyzing section 141 of the Act, it will be seen that it operates in cases where an offence under section 138 is committed by a Company. The key words which occur in the section are 'every person'. These are general words and take every person connected with a Company within their sweep. Therefore, these words have been rightly qualified by use of the words: 

 What is required is that the persons who are sought to be made criminally liable under section 141 should be, at the time the offence was committed, in charge of and responsible to the Company for the conduct of the business of the Company. Every person connected with the Company shall not fall within the ambit of the provision. It is only those persons who were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the Company at the time of commission of an offence, who will be liable for criminal action. It follows from this that if a director of a Company who was not in charge of and was not responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company at the relevant time, will not be liable under the provision. The liability arises from being in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the Company at the relevant time when the offence was committed and not on the basis of merely holding a designation or offence in a Company. Conversely, a person not holding any office or designation in a Company may be liable if he satisfies the main requirement of being in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of a Company at the relevant time. Liability depends on the role one plays in the affairs of a Company and not on designation or status. If being a director or manager or secretary was enough to cast criminal liability, the section would have said so. Instead of 'every person', the section would have said 'every director, manager or secretary in a Company is liable', etc. The Legislature is aware that it is a case of criminal liability which means serious consequence so far as the person sought to be made liable is concerned. Therefore, only persons who can be said to be connected with the commission of a crime at the relevant time have been subjected to action." 

 This paragraph 10 was quoted with approval by the Indian Supreme Court in the subsequent decision in the case of K Srikanth Sing vs North East Securities Ltd reported in 2007 (8) SCR 452 banked upon by Mr TH Khan. 

 (b) The answer to the question posed in para (b) has to be in the negative. Merely being a director of a Company is not sufficient to make the person liable under section 141 of the Act. A director in a Company cannot be deemed to be in charge of and responsible to the Company for the conduct of its business. The requirement of section 141 is that the person sought to be made liable should be in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company at the relevant time. This has to be averred as a fact as there is no deemed liability of a director in such cases. 

 35. In the decision in the case of Anil Hada vs Indian Acrylic Ltd reported in (2000)1 SCC 1, the Supreme Court of India held in paragraphs 11, 12 and 13: 

 13. If the offence was committed by a Company, it can be punished only if the Company is prosecuted. But instead of prosecuting the Company, if a payee opts to prosecute only the persons falling within the other categories, the payee can succeed in the case only if he succeeds in showing that the offence was actually committed by the Company. In such a prosecution, the accused can show that the Company has not committed the offence, though such Company is not made an accused, and hence the prosecuted accused is not liable to be punished. The provisions do not contain a condition that prosecution of the Company is sine qua non for prosecution of the other persons who fall within the other categories mentioned above. No doubt in a finding that the offence was committed by the Company is sine qua non for convicting those other persons. But if a Company is not prosecuted due to any legal snag or otherwise, the other prosecuted persons cannot, on that score alone, escape from the penal liability created through the legal fiction envisaged in section 141 of the Act." 

 In that case, eventually the Indian Supreme Court came to the conclusion that even if the prosecution proceedings against the Company were not taken or could not be continued, it is no bar to taking any proceeding against other persons falling within the purview 3: subsections (1) and (2) of section 141 of the Indian Negotiable Instruments Act. 

 36. In the decision in the case of Rajneesh Aggarwal vs Amit I Bhalla reported in 2001 SCC (CrI) 229, adverted to by Mr Md Iqbal Kabir, the Supreme Court of India observed in paragraph 6:— 

 So far as the first question is concerned, it is no doubt true that all the three requirements under clauses (a), (b) and (c) must be complied with before the offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act can be said to have been committed and section 141 indicates as to who would be the persons, liable in the event the offence is committed by a Company. The High Court itself, on facts, has recorded the findings that conditions (a) and (b) under section 138 having been duly complied with and, therefore, the only question is whether the conclusion of the High Court that condition (c) has not been complied with, can be said to be in accordance with law. Mere dishonour of a cheque would not give rise to a cause of action unless the payee makes a demand in writing to the drawer of the cheque for the payment and the drawer fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee. The cheques had been issued by M/s Bhalla Techtran Industries Limited, through its Director Shri Amit J Bhalla. The appellant had issued notice to said Shri Amit J Bhalla, Director of M/s Bhalla Techtran Industries Limited. Notwithstanding the service of the notice, the amount in question was not paid. The object of issuing notice indicating the factum of dishonour of the cheques is to give an opportunity to the drawer to make the payment within 15 days, so that it will not be necessary for the payee to proceed against in any criminal action, even though the bank dishonoured the cheques. It is Amit Bhalla, who had signed the cheques as the Director of M/s Bhalla Techtran Industries Ltd. When the notice was issued to said Shri Amit J Bhalla, Director of M/s Bhalla Techtran Industries Ltd, it was incumbent upon Shri Bhalla to see that the payments are made within the stipulated period of 15 days. It is not disputed (sic alleged) that Shri Bhalla has not signed the cheques, nor is it disputed (sic alleged) that Shri Bhalla was not the Director of the Company. Bearing in mind the object of issuance of such notice, it must be held that the notices cannot be construed in a narrow technical way without examining the substance of the matter. We really fail to understand as to why the judgment of this Court in Bilakchand Gyanchand Co will have no application. In that case also criminal proceedings had been initiated against A Chinnaswami, who was the Managing Director of the Company and the cheques in question had been signed by him. In the aforesaid premises, we have no hesitation to come to the conclusion that the High Court committed error in recording a finding that there was no notice to the drawer of the cheque, as required under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. In our opinion, after the cheques were dishonoured by the bank, the payee had served due notice and yet there was failure on the part of the accused to pay the money, who had signed the cheques, as the Director of the Company. The impugned Order of the High Court, therefore, is liable to be quashed." 

 37. In the decision in the case of M Venkateshwara Rao vs Medarametla Venkateshwaralu reported in 1984-1997 DCR (1) 416, the Andhra Pradesh High Court has held that without impleading the Company as an accused in a case under section 138 of the (Indian) Negotiable Instruments Act, the complaint is maintainable if the person who issued the cheque is made an accused. 

 38. In the decision in the case of Bimal Kumar Nopani vs State of Uttar Pradesh reported in 2006 (2) DCR 691, the Allahabad High Court has held that a person responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company could be prosecuted without prosecution of the Company itself and, as such, the complaint was maintainable. 

 39. In the decision in the case of UP Pollution Control Board vs Messrs Modi Distillery reported in 1987 SCC (Crl) 632, the Supreme Court of India dealt with the provisions of section 47 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. It may be mentioned that section 47 of the said Act deals with offences by companies. In that decision, the Supreme Court of India held in paragraph 6: 

 Although the observations made above pertain to a different law, namely, section 47 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 in the facts and circumstances of that case, yet in our estimation, the essence of those observations applies to the present case before 

 42. As to the contention of Mr TH Khan that non-opening of the letter of credit as per agreement dated 2-2-2009, the consideration has necessarily failed and, as such, the proceedings of the case are to be quashed, it seems that Mr Md Iqbal Kabir has rightly argued that is a matter of evidence and trial and the failure of the consideration, if any, can only be adjudicated upon at the trial on taking evidence to be adduced by the parties concerned. If for the sake of argument, we accept the above contention of Mr TH Khan right now, that will amount to begging the question. Furthermore, this is the defence version of the case. It is a settled proposition of law that the proceedings of a criminal case cannot be quashed on the basis of the defence materials [Rahela Khatun vs Abul Hassan; 48 DLR (AD) 213]. 

 44. Now a pertinent question arises: can the criminal case be proceeded with against the petitioners in the absence of such averment either in the petition of complaint or in the sworn statement recorded under section 200 of the Code? To our knowledge, there is no decision of our Appellate Division on this question. Anyway, it is the consensus judicial view of the Indian jurisdiction that it is the duty of the complainant to state therein as to how the petitioners were in charge of and were responsible for the conduct of the business of the Company. According to Mr Md Iqbal Kabir, this is a mere omission in the petition of complaint as well as in the sworn statement of the opposite-party No. 2. hi this context, the decision in the case of SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd vs Neeta Bhalla, reported in (2005) 8 SCC 89 by a larger Bench of the. Indian Supreme Court appears to be stimulating, thought-provoking and relishing. According to the 'ratio' of that decision, the petitioners can be proceeded against even in the absence of such averment either in the petition of complaint or in the sworn statement provided that they are signatories to the dishonoured cheque and their incriminating act is covered by the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 141 of the Indian Negotiable Instruments Act. 

 45. In the decision in the case of Anil Hada vs Indian Acrylic Ltd reported in (2000) 1 SCC 1, it has been clearly, unambiguously and categorically held that instead of prosecuting the Company, if a payee opts to prosecute only the persons falling within the other categories, the payee can succeed in the case only if he succeeds in showing that the offence was actually committed by the Company and the provisions do not contain a condition that prosecution of the Company is sine qua non for prosecution of the other persons who fall within those categories mentioned in section 141 of the Indian Negotiable Instruments Act. Besides, we have already touched upon the decisions of two Indian High Courts, namely, Andhra Pradesh High Court reported in 1984-1997 DCR (1) 416 and 2006 (2) DCR 691 respectively wherein their Lordships have found the complaints maintainable in the absence of the drawer-Company. However, there does not appear to be any decision of our Appellate Division on this point as well. 

 46. The most striking feature of the Indian Supreme Court decision reported in 2007 (8) SCR 452 adverted to by Mr TH Khan is that the same has not specifically dealt with the legal implications of non-impleading of the drawer-Company in a proceeding under section 138. In addition to that, this decision is silent as to the legal consequences of a dishonoured cheque signed by the accused for and on behalf of the Company. In our opinion, those aspects of the case have been exhaustively dealt with in the reference by the three-Judge Bench of the Indian Supreme Court in the decision reported in (2005) 8 SCC 89 (supra). 

 49. By the way, we feel tempted to advert to the unreported decision dated 10-7-2008 (to which one of us was a party) in the case of Md Farooq Hossain vs State, Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9760 of 2007. In that decision, it was spelt out: 

 "So it is ex-facie clear that under section 140(1) of the Act, the Company being an offender is to be made an accused along with the persons who were in charge of, and responsible to, the Company for the conduct of its business at the time of commission of the offence. The record shows that the cheque was issued by the petitioner and the co-accused on behalf of the Company. Be that as it may, it appears that at his own peril, the complainant-opposite-party No.2 has not made the Company, that is to say, Design Smith Limited an accused in the case. By not making the Company an accused in the case, the question of suffering any prejudice by the accused-petitioner does not arise at all. Rather it is the complainant-opposite-party No. 2 who may be prejudiced by his own action. Against this backdrop, the proceedings of the case cannot be quashed." 

 50. In the light of the discussion made above and having regard to the facts and circumstances of the instant case, we are led to hold that the petitioners being admitted signatories to the bounced cheque may be proceeded against under section 138 even in the absence of the Company (actual drawer) and their liability is covered by the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 140 of the Act of 1881. 

 53. It is undisputed that the Account No. 205-100-4086 with Dhaka Bank Limited is maintained by the Kaltimex, and not by the petitioners. It is nobody's case that the account belongs to the petitioners, though there is reference to that effect in the petition of complaint. This isolated reference in the petition of complaint, in our opinion, should not be blown up out of all proportion in any view of the matter. 

 54. From the foregoing discussion and in the facts and circumstances of the case, we find that no occasion has arisen for quashing the proceedings of the case pending in the Court below. It necessarily follows that the initiation and continuation of the proceedings of the case pending in the lower Court are not an abuse of the process of the Court. In this perspective, the question of quashing the proceedings of the case is out of the question. The Rule, therefore, fails. 

 56. The Court below is directed to proceed with the trial of the case in accordance with law.
